questions.question: Exact losses $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ have been recorded. Their specified independent observation model has density $f(x;\theta)$, with unknown parameter $\theta\in\Theta$. In maximum likelihood estimation, what varies in $L(\theta)=\prod_i f(x_i;\theta)$?
options: The losses vary; the parameter stays fixed.
The parameter varies; the recorded losses stay fixed.
Both vary to find the most likely possible sample.
Neither varies; the likelihood is one data probability.

questions.question: Independent exact observations $x_1,x_2$ have specified mass functions $p_1(x;\theta)$ and $p_2(x;\theta)$ sharing unknown parameter $\theta$. Their marginal laws need not match. Which likelihood construction is justified?
options: $L(\theta)=p_1(x_1;\theta)+p_2(x_2;\theta)$.
$L(\theta)=p_1(x_1;\theta)p_1(x_2;\theta)$.
A product is justified only if the marginal laws match.
$L(\theta)=p_1(x_1;\theta)p_2(x_2;\theta)$.

questions.question: One exact continuous loss $x$ is modelled by a specified density $f(x;\theta)$. For one admissible parameter the density value is $f(x;\theta)=2$. Why can this be a valid likelihood value?
options: It is a density height, rather than an exact-point probability.
It is a probability before division by the sample size.
It is invalid because every likelihood is at most one.
It means two observations occurred at the recorded point.

questions.question: Two admissible parameter candidates $a,b$ for fixed data have positive likelihoods $L(a)<L(b)$. Let $\ell(\theta)=\log L(\theta)$. Which ordering supports maximising $\ell$ instead of $L$?
options: $\ell(a)>\ell(b)$ whenever both likelihoods are below one.
$\ell(a)=\ell(b)$ because taking logs removes products.
$\ell(a)<\ell(b)$, even when both logs are negative.
$\ell(a)<\ell(b)$ only when both likelihoods exceed one.

questions.question: For fixed exact data, $L(\theta)=c(\theta)h(\theta)>0$ on parameter domain $\Theta$. A calculation proposes maximising $h$ alone. Which condition justifies discarding the factor $c$ for every such $h$?
options: The factor is positive but may depend on the parameter.
The factor contains none of the observed loss values.
The factor is a normalising term in the observation density.
The factor is a positive constant independent of the parameter.

questions.question: Three independent exact exponential losses are $2,3,5$, with rate $\lambda>0$ and density $f(x;\lambda)=\lambda \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}$ for $x>0$. What is the maximum likelihood rate estimate?
Independent observations $X_1,X_2$ take values zero or one, with $\mathbb{P}(X_i=1)=p$ and unknown $0<p<1$. The recorded pair is $(1,0)$. What is its likelihood as a function of $p$?
One exact positive loss $x=1$ has exponential density $f(x;\lambda)=\lambda \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}$ for rate $\lambda>0$. Compare candidates $\lambda=1$ and $\lambda=2$. What is $L(2)/L(1)$?

Two independent exponential losses are $1,1$, with rate $\lambda\in(0,1/2]$ and density $\lambda \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}$ for $x>0$. The unconstrained rate estimate is one. What is the constrained maximum likelihood estimate?

Independent exact losses $1,3$ have uniform density $f(x;\theta)=1/\theta$ for $0\le x\le\theta$ and zero otherwise, with unknown $\theta>0$. Which candidate must have zero likelihood because of the observed support?
options: $\theta=3$.
$\theta=4$.
$\theta=6$.
$\theta=2$.

questions.question: Independent exact observations $x_1,x_2$ have positive density factors $f_1=f(x_1;\theta)$ and $f_2=f(x_2;\theta)$ for unknown parameter $\theta$. Which expression is their log-likelihood?
options: $\log f_1+\log f_2$.
$\log f_1-\log f_2$.

questions.question: For one recorded success in a zero-or-one observation model, $\mathbb{P}_\theta(X=1)=\theta$ with $0\le\theta\le1$. Thus $L(\theta)=\theta$ and $\int_0^1L(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta=1/2$. Does this invalidate the likelihood?
options: Yes; double it and change the observation success probability.
No; a likelihood need not integrate to one over parameters.
Yes; only its logarithm is allowed to have nonunit integral.
No; the integral must be the probability of the recorded success.

questions.question: A specified observation model satisfies $f(x;a)=f(x;b)$ for every possible observation $x$ at two distinct admissible parameter values $a,b$. Exact observations are independent. If $a$ maximises their likelihood, what must hold for $b$?
options: It also maximises the same likelihood for these data.
It has a smaller likelihood because its parameter label differs.
It can be rejected by adding more independent observations.
It is ruled out because a maximum must be unique.

questions.question: Four independent zero-or-one observations all equal one. Their common success probability is $p\in[0,1]$, giving $L(p)=p^4$. Which maximum likelihood estimate is valid even though the positive likelihood has no interior stationary maximum?
options: $\hat p=0$.
$\hat p=1$.
No estimate exists without an interior derivative zero.

questions.question: Exact independent exponential losses $x_i>0$ have rate $\lambda>0$ and estimate $n/\sum_i x_i$. The same losses are re-expressed as $y_i=100x_i$ in smaller currency units. What is the rate estimate in the new units?
options: $\hat\lambda_y=100\hat\lambda_x$.
$\hat\lambda_y=\hat\lambda_x/100$.
$\hat\lambda_y=\hat\lambda_x$.
$\hat\lambda_y=\hat\lambda_x^2$.

questions.question: Independent exact losses $1,3$ have uniform density $1/\theta$ on $[0,\theta]$ and zero outside, with $\theta>0$. On its feasible domain $\theta\ge3$, the likelihood is $L(\theta)=\theta^{-2}$. Which estimate maximises the full likelihood?
options: $\hat\theta=2$.
$\hat\theta=4$.
$\hat\theta=\sqrt{5}$.
$\hat\theta=3$.

questions.question: One observation $X=1$ has model $\mathbb{P}_\theta(X=1)=1/4+(\theta-1/2)^2$ and the complementary mass at zero, for $0\le\theta\le1$. Its likelihood derivative is zero at $\theta=1/2$. What does checking the full objective show?
options: The stationary point is the unique maximum by its zero derivative.
Every parameter maximises because the masses sum to one.
The stationary point is a minimum; both endpoints maximise.
The right endpoint alone maximises because it is largest.

questions.question: One exact continuous loss is $x=1$. For each parameter $\theta$, two specified densities agree everywhere except at $x=1$, where they assign different heights. How can this affect an exact-data likelihood despite describing the same observation law?
options: The likelihood height can change although all interval probabilities agree.
The likelihood cannot change because singleton probabilities are zero.
An interval probability changes by the difference in singleton heights.
Only one density is valid because a density fixes every point uniquely.

questions.question: Let $X_1=X_2=Z$, where $Z$ equals one with probability $p\in(0,1)$ and zero otherwise. Both recorded values are one. At $p=1/2$, what is their joint likelihood, and what error gives a different value?
options: $1/4; dependence does not change equal marginal masses$.
$1; adding the two success masses gives the joint event$.
$1/8; the latent value supplies a third independent draw$.
$1/2; treating the copies as independent gives 1/4$.

questions.question: Three independent zero-or-one observations all equal one, with common success probability $p$ restricted to the open domain $0<p<1$. Their likelihood is $L(p)=p^3$. Which statement correctly diagnoses existence of a maximum likelihood estimate?
options: The estimate is one because it is the largest boundary value.
No maximum is attained; likelihood approaches one as p approaches one.
The estimate is zero because the derivative has a boundary root.
The estimate is one half because the parameter interval is open.
